Security Threat Modeling for Emerging AI-Agent Protocols: A Comparative Analysis of MCP, A2A, Agora, and ANP

Zeynab Anbiaee Email: saba.anbiaee@unb.ca Address: Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity (CIC), University of New Brunswick, New Brunswick, Canada. Corresponding author: Corresponding author    Mahdi Rabbani Email: m.rabbani@unb.ca Address: Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity (CIC), University of New Brunswick, New Brunswick, Canada.    Mansur Mirani Email: mansur.mirani@mastercard.com Address: Mastercard Vancouver Tech Hub, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada.    Gunjan Piya Email: sunny.piya@mastercard.com Address: Mastercard Vancouver Tech Hub, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada.    Igor Opushnyev Email: igor.opushnyev@mastercard.com Address: Mastercard Vancouver Tech Hub, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada.    Ali Ghorbani Email: ghorbani@unb.ca Address: Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity (CIC), University of New Brunswick, New Brunswick, Canada.    Sajjad Dadkhah Email: sdadkhah@unb.ca Address: Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity (CIC), University of New Brunswick, New Brunswick, Canada.
Abstract

The rapid development of the AI agent communication protocols, including the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Agent2Agent (A2A), Agora, and Agent Network Protocol (ANP), is reshaping how AI agents communicate with tools, services, and each other. While these protocols support scalable multi-agent interaction and cross-organizational interoperability, their security principles remain understudied, and standardized threat modeling is limited; no protocol-centric risk assessment framework has been established yet. This paper presents a systematic security analysis of four emerging AI agent communication protocols. First, we develop a structured threat modeling analysis that examines protocol architectures, trust assumptions, interaction patterns, and lifecycle behaviors to identify protocol-specific and cross-protocol risk surfaces. Second, we introduce a qualitative risk assessment framework that identifies twelve protocol-level risks and evaluates security posture across the creation, operation, and update phases through systematic assessment of likelihood, impact, and overall protocol risk, with implications for secure deployment and future standardization. Third, we provide a measurement-driven case study on MCP that formalizes the risk of missing mandatory validation/attestation for executable components as a falsifiable security claim by quantifying wrong-provider tool execution under multi-server composition across representative resolver policies. Collectively, our results highlight key design-induced risk surfaces and provide actionable guidance for secure deployment and future standardization of agent communication ecosystems.

Keywords: 
Model Context Protocol (MCP), Agent2Agent Protocol (A2A), Agent Network Protocol (ANP), Agora protocol, Risk Assessment, AI agent Security, Threat modeling, Secure AI Integration.

1 Introduction

For decades, neuroscientists, mathematicians, and many other scientists tried to make the systems intelligent, and finally, Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) arose. The real journey of AI started with symbolic AI and expert systems, which were rule-based and rigid [48]. Then ML came for enabling systems to learn patterns from data rather than relying on hard-coded rules [11]. As data and computational power grew, deep learning emerged, giving rise to powerful models for vision, speech, and more. That evolution led to large language models (LLMs), which understand and generate human language at scale [38, 21]. But now, it is time for a new phase: the age of AI agents. These are not just passive models waiting for user prompts; they are proactive and autonomous entities capable of interacting with tools, environments, and other AI agents [35, 39]. Providing secure and structured communication between AI agents is a foundation for what’s next: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) [29] and even Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) [29], where intelligent agents collaborate seamlessly in real-time environments [16]. Figure 1 shows where we are now and highlights that communication protocols are not just tools for today; they are the logical next step in this evolution. In the future, the AGI era will come when AI can reason, learn, and adapt like a human across any task. At the ASI age, AI surpasses human intelligence in every meaningful way.

The rapid advancement of agentic AI in 2025 further accelerated this transition. The integration of autonomous agents with LLMs enhanced system capabilities in complex reasoning, tool invocation, and inter-agent communication [35, 5]. These agents, powered by core LLMs such as GPT, Claude, and others, serve as the foundation of intelligent systems capable of interacting with external APIs, retrieving information from knowledge bases, and negotiating with other agents to fulfill the intent of a user’s prompt [39]. This architecture transforms LLMs from passive responders into dynamic, goal-driven entities operating within multi-agent ecosystems [35]. A broader systemic transition is expected in 2026, as more companies and organizations begin reshaping their systems to become agent-ready. This means going beyond traditional software design to ensure that backend services can be accessed by autonomous AI agents. Additionally, it will require the integration of context-aware access controls, robust tool invocation frameworks, and protocol support for structured agent communication to ensure safe, reliable, and scalable agent-driven operations [16].

From a security and privacy perspective, however, this evolution poses significant challenges, particularly given that cybersecurity mechanisms are not evolving at the same pace as agentic AI systems. Security teams are still grappling with new threats introduced by LLMs between 2023 and 2025, including prompt injection, context manipulation, unauthorized tool execution, and AI-driven social engineering [10, 31]. Traditional data security frameworks centered on confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA) are no longer sufficient in AI agent environments. Instead, these principles must be reinterpreted in a context-sensitive manner, shifting toward context confidentiality, context integrity, and context availability [34]. This adaptation emphasizes the need to secure the evolving, dynamic, and often short-lived context windows that support reasoning, coordination, and decision making in multi agent-systems.

Securing these complex communication processes requires a systematic investigation of vulnerabilities in the communication protocols used by agentic AI systems. Limited awareness of protocol-level interactions and dependencies directly affects exposure surfaces, trust boundaries, and failure propagation across multi-agent workflows. However, existing studies remain fragmented and largely focus on isolated protocol risks or specific implementations, without offering a unified view of vulnerability classes across agent communication layers [16, 34].

To address this gap, this paper advances the emerging area of AI-agent protocol security through a systematic and forward-looking analysis of communication risks in agentic ecosystems. Although each emerging protocol in the literature follows a different architecture and introduces its own set of vulnerabilities that require independent analysis, examining isolated weaknesses alone is not sufficient to capture system-level risks. Instead, this paper provides a protocol-centric perspective that integrates threat modeling, architectural analysis, and lifecycle-aware risk assessment across multiple emerging protocols, and offers a structured basis for comparative evaluation and proactive mitigation. The selection of the four communication protocols is primarily based on two criteria: popularity and maturity [51]. Among many emerging standardization efforts, these protocols have progressed beyond conceptual proposals and have begun to see practical integration, making them suitable for systematic security analysis. The contributions of this paper are as follows:

  • •

    We present a structured, comparative security threat modeling analysis of MCP, A2A, ANP, and Agora, consolidating scattered early findings and protocol documentation into a coherent taxonomy that highlights risk surfaces under realistic deployment assumptions.

  • •

    We perform an architecture-based analysis and derive a catalog of design-induced threat hypotheses for MCP, A2A, ANP, and Agora, grounded in trust boundaries, identity/authorization binding assumptions, and cross-protocol composition risks.

  • •

    We present a systematic qualitative risk assessment of major AI agent communication protocols, identifying twelve protocol-level risks and proposing a lifecycle-aware framework that evaluates security posture across the creation, operation, and update phases, with implications for secure deployment and future standardization.

  • •

    We contribute a measurement-driven case study that formalizes the lack of mandatory validation or attestation for executable components in MCP as a falsifiable security claim by quantifying wrong-provider tool execution under multi-server composition across multiple realistic resolver policies.

This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on agent communication and protocol security. Section 3 introduces the foundations of agent communication protocols and representative frameworks. Section 4 presents the threat model and key security dimensions. Section 5 analyzes potential threats arising from protocol design and system architecture. Section 6 describes the evaluation methodology and assessment framework. Section 7 provides an experimental case study to demonstrate the applicability of the proposed analysis framework on real-world agent communication protocols. Section 8 concludes the paper and summarizes the main findings. Finally, Section 9 discusses future research directions. Figure 2 provides a high-level overview of the paper’s organization, including its main sections and subsections.

2 Related Work

Research on the security and privacy of AI systems has expanded rapidly with the fast deployment of LLMs [24]. As these models move beyond standalone usage and become embedded in systems, understanding how existing threats evolve and how new risks emerge has become increasingly important [10]. Although concerns related to LLMs are not new, many studies in the literature have already examined the privacy and security issues associated with standalone LLM models [52]. More recently, as LLMs have been integrated with external resources through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), these privacy and security concerns have become even more complex [53]. In this survey, the focus is on a mature form of agentic AI in which all major components are present, including the LLM, orchestration mechanisms, and multiple agents operating under coordinated control [26]. This also includes user–agent interactions, agent–agent negotiation, and agent–environment interactions [45]. This survey is among the first to take a broad view of this entire ecosystem in order to highlight existing vulnerabilities and discuss potential risks that are likely to emerge as these systems continue to evolve.

In early 2025, as the use of AI agents and, more broadly, agentic AI systems became more familiar to both research communities and industry, several communication protocols were proposed to support coordination among agents [7]. Most of these protocols remain at a conceptual stage and have not yet been fully implemented or evaluated in real-world environments [51]. Therefore, this survey focuses on four relatively mature and most popular protocols, MCP, A2A, Agora, and ANP, for detailed analysis, in order to provide a focused and practical discussion aligned with current development [41].

To the best of current knowledge, this study represents one of the first efforts to conduct risk assessment and security threat modeling across agentic AI communication protocols. For comparison with related works in the literature, studies with high relevance as well as those with moderate relevance to security and privacy in AI agent communication are considered. Table 1 provides a concise comparison of existing related works and highlights how the identified gaps are addressed in this paper through risk assessment and threat prediction across the four main AI agent protocols.

2.1 Security Studies on MCP Communication Protocols

In the last two years, researchers have approached security for the MCP from several angles, though none have yet delivered a fully formal threat model. Hou and colleagues [25] offer the first deep dive into MCP’s architecture and operation. They break the server life cycle into three stages, including creation, operation, and update, then walk through the kinds of problems that can arise at each step. The study assumes a semi-trusted environment in which MCP components behave as specified but considers the presence of malicious servers, tools, and installers in the broader ecosystem. The security model is an informal, risk-based one that analyzes threats in the server lifecycle without defining a formal adversary model, and the primary contribution is in identifying threats at the ecosystem level.

Narajala et al. [37] adopt a different approach by treating all MCP components (client, server, and host) as untrusted and constructing a defense-in-depth security framework under a Zero-Trust assumption. By systematically cataloging attack vectors, they derive concrete controls for authentication, authorization, and continuous monitoring. While the proposed layered mitigations and Zero-Trust design patterns provide useful guidance, the authors acknowledge that the recommendations have not been empirically evaluated nor enforced at the protocol level. Ehtesham et al. [16] present a taxonomy, comparative analysis, and roadmap for AI agent communication protocols, rather than proposing new security mechanisms or formally assessing attack surfaces. A key limitation is that security is treated descriptively and per-protocol, and not systematically threat-modeled, in terms of cross-protocol attack analysis, or through empirical validation in conditions of malicious multi-agent interaction.

Another work examines MCP outside of a security context. Yang et al. [50] integrate MCP servers in IoT environments using edge devices and evaluate protocol performance in such settings, but provide little discussion of security. Conversely, few design-oriented studies focus on protecting integrity during installation by advocating cryptographic integrity checks, code-hash verification, manifest signing, and checksums to detect tampering with tools and servers [50], [32]. While these measures strengthen the installation phase, they do not address runtime attacks nor provide a comprehensive threat model for the MCP ecosystem.

Taken together, these studies indicate that researchers have begun to identify risks and propose safeguards for MCP, ranging from lifecycle-based risk analyses to enterprise-oriented hardening frameworks. However, the field still lacks formal adversary models, empirical attack-based evaluations, and cross-protocol analysis, leaving substantial scope for more rigorous and systematic security research on MCP.

2.2 Security Studies on A2A Communication Protocols

Google’s A2A protocol has become a prominent standard for coordinating multiple AI agents, but its security implications remain an active research area. A case study by Duan and Lu [13] assesses the A2A protocol for edge-computing environments, noting that edge-based multi-agent systems face heterogeneity, scalability, dynamicity, and resource constraints; their analysis shows that the A2A Agent Card mechanism helps address heterogeneity but lacks a standard schema to capture host-level resource information. Habler et al. [20] analyze the security of A2A using the MAESTRO threat-modeling framework, with emphasis on vulnerabilities in Agent Card management, task-execution integrity, and authentication, and propose secure development practices. Nevertheless, the analysis is limited to application-level threats and does not address protocol-level threats inherent to A2A.

Louck et al. [33] provide recommendations to enhance the A2A protocol for handling sensitive data in multi-agent workflows. The authors propose protocol-level refinements; however, these remain largely conceptual and example-driven, without attack-based evaluation, formal security guarantees, or assessment of scalability and performance overhead. In addition, they identify critical weaknesses in A2A, including insufficient token-lifetime controls, lack of strong customer authentication, and over-broad access scopes. Empirical prompt-injection tests indicate that the proposed refinements can reduce sensitive-data leakage while maintaining low latency.

Beyond protocol analysis, a broader multi-agent security study by He et al. [23] shows that vulnerabilities in individual components can cascade through inter-agent communications, illustrating that rigorous threat modeling and benchmarking are necessary for trustworthy multi-agent systems. A2A has also been extended to specific domains: Duan et al. [15] propose an AI-Agent Communication Network (ACN) for 6G environments where security is treated as an inherent property of the underlying network, rather than being addressed at the protocol level; other works examine A2A’s use in edge-computing scenarios, focusing on scalability and heterogeneity rather than explicit threat analysis.

In summary, these studies underscore that while A2A provides a foundational communication framework, robust security requires formal threat models, cryptographic enhancements, and empirical validation.

2.3 Other Protocols and Related Studies

In addition to MCP and A2A, two other protocols, ANP [8] and Agora [36], are frequently discussed in the emerging literature on agent communication. These protocols are considered in this survey because they adopt different architectural assumptions and interaction models, which introduce distinct security challenges. However, compared to MCP and A2A, security and privacy analyses for ANP and Agora remain relatively limited and largely design-oriented.

Existing research on Agora primarily emphasizes communication efficiency, scalability, and flexible coordination among large numbers of LLM-driven agents [36]. The design assumes a cooperative and non-adversarial environment and does not define an explicit threat model. Consequently, critical security aspects such as agent authentication, authorization, resistance to malicious agents, protocol abuse, and data exfiltration are not systematically examined. Similarly, ANP is primarily specified through architectural designs and technical specifications that emphasize decentralized identity, encrypted communication, and interoperability [8]. While these features suggest built-in security considerations, existing work does not provide formal adversary models, protocol-level attack analyses, or empirical validation under malicious multi-agent conditions. Overall, studies on ANP and Agora currently lack rigorous security assessments, formal threat modeling, and experimental evaluation under adversarial conditions. This gap further motivates the need for protocol-centric and ecosystem-level security analysis across heterogeneous agent communication standards.

Beyond MCP, A2A, ANP, and Agora, existing studies are fragmented and tend to focus on individual components or isolated interaction patterns, rather than offering a holistic security and privacy perspective on the agent communication protocol ecosystem. Kong et al. [30] provide a survey for LLM-driven agent communication; they introduce a three-class taxonomy, analyse security risks at each communication layer, and perform experiments using MCP and A2A to illustrate potential vulnerabilities, and offer defense countermeasures. Zhang et al. [54] review LLM-based multi-agent systems across capabilities, collaboration, architectures, communication, and applications. However, security is treated only at a high level, without formal threat models or protocol-level validation.

In the domain of the Internet of Agents (IoA), some studies have explored agent-centric communication and collaboration frameworks. Wang et al. [47] examine identity authentication, cross-agent trust, embodied security, and privacy risks in IoA systems. It highlights the need for resilient defenses against agent forgery, intent deception, collusion, and prompt-injection attacks; however, the proposed security model is primarily taxonomic and descriptive, with no mechanisms for formal enforcement and operational guarantees. In a related survey, the same authors [46] introduce an agent-centric infrastructure that enables interconnection, discovery, and collaboration among agents. Their survey presents a hierarchical IoA architecture and discusses key enablers such as agent discovery, adaptive communication, task matching, consensus, and incentive mechanisms. However, security and privacy are mainly discussed at a conceptual level, without formal threat models or protocol-level enforcement mechanisms. Additional discussions on AI agent communication frameworks in IoT environments can be found in [19] and [14], though these works do not focus on general-purpose agent communication protocols.

Yan et al. [49] explored LLM-based multi-agent systems from a communication-centric perspective, analyzing system level and internal communication mechanisms and discussing challenges such as efficiency, scalability, and security. However, security is addressed mainly at a conceptual level, without formal threat models or protocol-level validation. Authors of [43] argue that ecosystem fragmentation threatens agentic AI and propose a Web of Agents architecture comprising agent-to-agent messaging, interaction interoperability, state management, and agent discovery; however, they overlooked defining threat models and protocol specifications. Yang et al. [51] provide a comprehensive review of AI agent communication protocols, categorizing protocols into two dimensions: context-oriented versus inter-agent and general-purpose versus domain-specific. They assume that agents, tools, and protocols behave based on their specifications, and the issue of adversarial agents is not investigated. The authors consider security as one of the dimensions of the assessment, but without threat models and adversarial scenarios.

Overall, these works highlight the urgency of developing secure, interoperable agent ecosystems but often lack formalized adversary models or empirical validation. Continued research is needed to bridge protocol design with security analysis and practical mitigation strategies.

3 Foundations of Agent Communication Protocols

AI assistants have become popular but are limited by their isolation from data and what they were trained on. Without access to external tools and data sources, they are restricted in providing updated data, acting in the real world, and connecting to external systems. AI agent protocols address this challenge by providing universal materials and interfaces for connecting AI systems with data sources and other AI agents.

The AI agent protocols are standard communication frameworks that specify how agents communicate with tools, resources, and other agents. They define message structures, authentication and authorization procedures, reporting of errors, and how the work should be coordinated across heterogeneous environments.

3.1 Historical Context and Evolution

The evolution of agent communication protocols requires collaboration and scalability of AI systems. Early AI assistants (2020-2022) were limited to proprietary platforms and, while they offered many advantages, had significant weaknesses, such as the absence of inter-system integration and redundant logins and authentication transactions.

By 2023, open-source frameworks such as LangChain and AutoGPT had emerged, demonstrating the importance of standard, secure, and consistent communication layers to support tool invocation, context sharing, and multi-agent collaboration. Since 2024, a new phase in the evolution of AI agent protocols has begun. Anthropic introduced MCP as the first open protocol to enable the connection of AI agents and external resources. At the same time, research groups announced the idea of Agora, which addresses the triad of agent communication (adaptability, efficiency, and portability). In 2025, Google launched the A2A protocol, and ANP emerged to predict the internet of agents at a large scale. The combination of these protocols suggests a migration towards secure and interactive systems of agent collaboration.

3.2 Model Context Protocol (MCP)

In 2024, Anthropic introduced MCP as a new open standard protocol for connecting AI agents [3]. It is open-source and platform-agnostic, enabling agents to have a two-way connection with external tools and facilitating complex workflows. Figure 3 shows the benefit of using MCP in decreasing the complexity and increasing the scalability of AI agent ecosystems. MCP helps developers avoid fragmented integration and maintain a standard integrated connection to data sources.

The MCP host, MCP client, and MCP server are the three main components of the MCP architecture that provide a smooth connection between data sources and AI applications. In a normal workflow, as depicted in Figure 4, the user sends a request prompt to the MCP client to evaluate the context, then the MCP server chooses the relevant tools and calls external APIs to obtain and process the data.

The MCP host is an AI application that hosts the MCP client and offers the environment for executing AI-based operations. It combines data and interactive features to facilitate seamless contact with external services and enhances connectivity with external MCP servers.

The MCP client serves as a mediator that controls communication between the MCP host and the MCP servers. It sends requests to MCP servers and asks about the functionalities that are available, then gets answers about the server’s capabilities that guarantee smooth communication with the external tools. Moreover, the MCP client handles alerts from MCP servers and manages requests and responses.

The MCP server, which is responsible for managing and providing AI models with the resources, has three phases: creation, operation, and update. Each phase defines activities for secure and efficient functions [25]. The creation step is the first phase that registers and configures the server. Then, in the operation phase, the MCP server processes requests, invokes appropriate tools, handles multiple slash commands while preventing conflicts, and enforces a sandbox mechanism to ensure an isolated, secure execution environment. In the last phase, the MCP server maintains security and adaptability by verifying post-update access permissions.

The MCP server defines three core components that enhance AI model operations, including Tools, Resources, and Prompts. Tools allow MCP servers to use a common supply-and-consumption model to automatically call external services and APIs. Resources facilitate data-driven decision-making and give AI models access to structured or unstructured datasets from local storage, databases, or cloud sources. Prompts are predefined templates or workflows for maximizing answers and guaranteeing consistency.

3.3 Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol

In April 2025, Google, with contributions from several technology partners such as Langchain and PayPal, introduced a new open protocol that complements MCP, called A2A [44]. The A2A protocol allows AI agents to communicate and exchange information securely and coordinate actions across different organizational platforms or applications, regardless of their underlying technologies. It is built on existing common standards, including Server-Sent Events (SSE), HTTP(S), and JSON-RPC, meaning it is easier to integrate with existing IT stacks and is designed to support enterprise-level authentication and authorization. A2A uses OAuth 2.0 [22] for mutual agent authentication and access to resources without sharing credentials; it also uses JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) [28] for compacting and signing tokens, smoothing secure transmission of authentication between agents, and ensuring integrity and verification of access [33].

The A2A protocol provides structured and bidirectional communication between a client agent and a remote agent to distribute task execution. Within this framework, the client agent formulates tasks and transmits them to the remote agent, then the remote agent works on the tasks to collect the correct information.

Agents advertise their functional capabilities through a standardized Agent Card in JSON format to enable the client agent to find the most relevant remote agent for a given task, thereby optimizing task allocation and execution. In addition, tasks are encapsulated within a well-defined protocol object that has a life cycle. The protocol supports both synchronous completion and asynchronous execution for long-running processes. In the latter case, periodic status updates maintain synchronization between agents. The task’s final output is formalized as an artifact, ensuring structured result handling. Agents can exchange contextual messages, intermediate responses, artifacts, and user instructions to keep alignment during task execution [1]. By this mechanism, A2A provides a flexible communication platform that supports interoperability, maintains execution context, and optimizes distributed agent collaboration. Figure 5 shows A2A protocol components and workflow.

3.4 Agora Protocol

Agora [36] is an agent communication protocol built to solve the Agent Communication Trilemma in heterogeneous LLM networks. That trilemma captures the fact that versatility (support for diverse message formats and modalities), efficiency (low computational and network costs), and portability (ease of implementation and deployment with minimal human intervention) are inherently incompatible; trying to have a system optimized in all of these dimensions is difficult. Many older solutions enhance one of these dimensions at the cost of the others; by making a protocol more versatile, one can usually increase computational overheads and make a deployment more difficult.

Agora uses the capabilities of LLM in natural language comprehension, code generation, and self-learning protocol negotiation to adjust communication tactics to the context. Its main novelty lies in the use of Protocol Documents (PDs) that allow autonomous agents to negotiate, adapt, and modify protocols, and in some cases, even develop new communication protocols with zero human interaction. Agents share PDs that are a uniquely identified solution with decentralized storage and retrieval and no central authorities, enabling reuse across agents that have never interacted.

Agora has a technology-agnostic design and is a Layer Zero protocol that sits above implementation, communications, and physical layers. The meta-protocol layer is responsible for enabling adaptive and negotiable communication through PDs. With this abstraction, Agora separates protocol logic from implementations and makes a technology-agnostic basis for agent communication. Figure 6 provides a conceptual layered abstraction of the Agora protocol.

Incorporating both structured and natural language, Agora presents a workable balance between versatility and efficiency. In the meantime, it is enhancing portability and flexibility for large, heterogeneous agent networks.

3.5 Agent Network Protocol (ANP)

ANP [8] [18] is an open standard for providing network interoperability between autonomous agents in heterogeneous environments. Stimulated by the development of the human communication networks towards the Internet, ANP imagines the IoA as a global, secure, and efficient environment to collaborate with billions of machine entities. The ANP design aims at eliminating data silos, facilitating connectivity between agents, and providing high efficiency in machine-to-machine communication (M2M).

ANP is based on three foundational principles; the first one is interconnectivity, which means the agents should be able to completely share the contextual information in an interchange method in an obstruction-free manner. The second principle is native interfaces, which means the agents may interact more readily by using APIs and uniform protocols rather than human-centric interfaces such as graphical interfaces and manually entered information. Last but not least is efficient collaboration that agents can create and take part in ad hoc networks and role negotiation autonomously by the use of automatic organization and automatic negotiation approaches.

The architecture of the protocol has three layers. The Identity and Encrypted Communication layer integrates the W3C Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) framework in order to support decentralized authentication, allowing trustless, end-to-end encrypted communication between different agents across different platforms. The Meta-Protocol layer is meant to act as a protocol of protocols where agents may negotiate which communication standard (examples include Agora [36]) to apply to a certain interaction accordingly. Lastly, the Application Protocol Layer defines agent discovery mechanisms, descriptions of capabilities, and execution of tasks in domain-related situations [2]. Figure 7. demonstrates the layered architecture of ANP with its identity, meta-protocol, and application layers, along with their core components.

The functional cycle starts with a local agent submitting a standardized search application to a standard discovery process to find a list of available agents. The agent would then access description files about the capabilities of the discovered agents and interfaces and what is needed in order to authenticate itself. On this basis, the initiating agent builds and delivers authenticated requests and processes the responses to accomplish collaborative tasks. Tables 2 and 3 summarize all the information provided in this section.

4 Threat Model

Deploying AI agent communication protocols introduces a wide range of new risks because, unlike traditional systems, these protocols allow agents, tools, and external resources to interact in an autonomous and multi-step manner. These capabilities increase the attack surface and open up new attack vectors. This section presents the reported security threats in AI agent protocols, which are extracted from [33], [25], [51], [6], [40].

The taxonomy is organized by impact domain: security threats address authentication, supply chain, and operational integrity. This structure ensures clarity, avoids redundancy, and aligns with established models such as STRIDE and the CIA triad. The Authentication & Access Control group of attacks undermines the reliability of agent identity, credential validation, and access enforcement, which are the foundation of secure collaboration across protocols. The Supply Chain & Ecosystem Integrity group compromises the integrity of AI ecosystem artifacts and update chains, mirroring modern supply-chain risks in decentralized ecosystems. And the Operational Integrity & Reliability group targets the stable execution and interpretation of tasks across dynamic agent networks, affecting integrity, availability, and coordination reliability. The taxonomy is shown in Figure 8. The summarization of all the attacks is provided in Table 4.

4.1 Authentication and Access Control

4.1.1 Lack of authentication

: The early version of MCP v1.0 did not have authentication mechanisms; hence, it was prone to impersonation and spoofing until a later update (MCP v1.2) added token-based authentication that guaranteed the integrity of data transmission and identity verification trustworthiness.

4.1.2 Weak or limited access control

: Role or Access Control List (ACL) granularity is desired since MCP lacks fine-grained permissions. Coarse permissions fail to add restrictions at the field, endpoint, or task level and expose systems to unpermitted access and privilege escalation.

4.1.3 Naming Collision & Impersonation

In the creation stage of MCP, once a malicious entity registers an MCP server with a name close to a known one (i.e., mcp-github vs github-mcp), it can impersonate clients and agents. MCP clients discover servers by simply reading their description and name, rather than cryptographic evidence. In decentralized, community-driven environments, there is no central registry to enforce naming rules. A malicious server misleads AI agents into invoking the fake server and gets access to sensitive data, executes unauthorized commands, and disrupts workflows. At this time, MCP operates locally, but in the future, in multitenant environments, the risk of name attack will increase. These challenges highlight the need for centralized management for name registration. Indeed, the lack of a namespace construct in MCP is a root cause that increases both collision likelihood and command-level ambiguity.

4.1.4 Absence of limitations on token lifetime

A2A uses OAuth 2.0 for authentication, but does not impose strict expiration durations of tokens for sensitive operations. Consequently, the leaked or intercepted tokens can be stored for hours or even days, allowing the attackers to reuse them to replay or to gain unauthorized access. The issue is even more critical in asynchronous long-lived workflows when the agents of an organization interact with each other. In the absence of cryptographically shortened lifetimes or single-use tokens, the protocol provides a wide attack window. This has been noted in other distributed systems involving similar distributed systems, in which revoked or expired tokens were accepted, and the need to closely associate token lifetimes with particular actions and time boundaries.

4.1.5 Insufficiently Granular Token Scopes

Tokens in the A2A are typically coarse-grained, so they give agents more privileges than they need in their respective work. As an example, a token that was supposed to be used for a single payment might allow access to other unrelated resources accidentally. This coarse scoping leaves a vulnerability to privilege escalation, with all tokens being compromised, allowing attackers to expand their access to areas not originally referenced. Security-wise, this compromises the principle of least privilege and subjects sensitive workflows to exploitation.

4.2 Supply Chain and Ecosystem Integrity

4.2.1 Installer Spoofing

During the creation phase, attackers are able to publish altered installers or one-click setup programs (e.g., mcp-get, mcp-installer) that install malware or backdoors. Many users, to do so conveniently, have a tendency to use non-official community installers, which do not verify packages or signatures. Attackers can have long-term access, exfiltrate credentials, or reconfigure servers by means of malicious installers. MCP is a much more community-driven system; that means that the attack surface is massive and largely uncontrolled.

4.2.2 Code Injection and Backdoors

MCP servers are often open-source and rely on community-maintained libraries. In addition, malicious or compromised dependencies introduce backdoors into MCP servers. In this regard, without rigorous dependency checks or reproducible builds, attackers can slip in code-level exploits. After an MCP server is compromised, it leaves behind a backdoor, which survives updates and can silently steal data, increase privileges, or interfere with operations. Unlike Installer spoofing, which is related to the initial delivery/bootstrapping stage of the supply chain, this vector concerns the payload/persistence stage after installation.

4.2.3 Tool Poisoning

Tools within the MCP ecosystem, especially in the operation phase, can have the same or misleadingly similar names. Besides, MCP enables agents to independently choose the tools according to the names and descriptions. In the case that a malicious tool is given a name or description in order to seem more pertinent, the client may prioritize it. The result is a toolflow hijacking in which attackers trick the MCP client into invoking their tool instead of the intended one, thereby possibly stealing sensitive data or executing malicious code.

4.2.4 Rug Pulls

Rug-pull attacks are a kind of risk in which, at first, adversarial tools or agents act appropriately to gain trust and be integrated into the workflows of critical operations. When the dependency has been established, the malicious party changes their behavior, either removing the desired functionality or adding some bad behavior. MCP and A2A promote dynamic discovery and healthy relationships; therefore, rug pulls are a serious threat to integrity and dependability. Their malicious character lies in the fact that they are activated later, and when they are used, they can bypass the initial checks and use the developed trust relations.

4.3 Operational Integrity and Reliability

4.3.1 Slash Command Overlap

The flexible multi-tool environment promoted at MCP provides significant extensibility, yet does not have powerful disambiguation. Several tools define the same or similar slash commands (e.g., /delete), which threatened the system integrity during the operation phase. In this state, an attacker can insert an incompatible command and cause the MCP client to take unwanted actions (e.g., deleting logs rather than temporary files). This compromises operational reliability and may lead to loss of data.

4.3.2 Sandbox Escape

MCP is based on the local isolation or containerization operation at the operation stage. In case the sandbox implementation contains unpatched vulnerabilities, e.g., system calls or runtime libraries, malicious tools may breach isolation. Indeed, attackers would be able to run arbitrary code on the host, get sensitive system data, or escalate privileges. This is a systemic risk in the enterprise deployment since MCP hosts generally have wide access to tools and resources.

4.3.3 Shadowing Attacks

A less severe form of tool poisoning is the shadowing attack, in which malicious actors pretend to be legitimate tools or agents but shadow these agents during their execution. Using this method, the shadowing entity redirects traffic and intercepts workflows, and finally replaces malicious results or modifies outputs. This attack exploits decentralized discovery and can silently corrupt a multi-agent workflow in MCP and A2A protocols.

4.3.4 Post-Update Privilege Persistence

Post-update privilege persistence is a vulnerability that is critical and occurs when outdated privileges or revoked privileges are still valid after an MCP server update. This issue arises as the updates to privilege are not always replicated across all server instances or invalidated as part of the updating process (e.g., API key revocations, permission changes, or role updates). This may provide adversaries with an opportunity to abuse residual privileges to conduct malicious activities, steal sensitive resources, or cause a system malfunction.

4.3.5 Re-deployment of Vulnerable Versions

The probability of redeploying susceptible MCP versions is due to the community-based and decentralized character of the ecosystem. There is no official package management infrastructure or auditing authority to impose the use of secure versions. This leaves a dangerous window between the disclosure of vulnerability and its adoption by a patch system, where attackers can still take advantage of vulnerabilities that are already known. In this condition, a malicious actor could deliberately attack organizations that have older MCP servers to gain higher privileges or interfere with the server operations.

4.3.6 Configuration Drift

It is defined as the gradual build-up of unwanted configuration drift that goes against a secure configuration. This issue is particularly acute in MCP environments, where end-users localize a server or it is deployed in ecosystems that are community-driven. It is dangerous to individual local deployments, but it is even more severe with remote or cloud MCP services, like those provided by Cloudflare, where configuration errors can affect more than one user or organization at a time. In a multi-tenant environment, one drift event may accidentally reveal sensitive resources, escalate privileges, or extend access to attackers across tenants.

This section discusses the threats that are reported in the other literature as the weaknesses of AI agent protocols, and most of them refer to the MCP and A2A communication. Based on our searches, no reported security analysis has been published on ANP or Agora either. This is not a surprise: all four protocols are young and still at an initial stage of development and implementation, and the academic community has only just started to discuss their security aspects. As a result, the attacks reported so far are not comprehensive and do not represent the full range of threats posed by the architecture, trust assumptions, and interoperability features of these new ecosystems.

Since the AI-agent protocols are new and are changing fast, it is vital to go beyond what is already being reported and actively investigate structurally possible attack vectors before they become real in deployment. To address this problem, the next section provides further analysis and presents a collection of deduced, architecture-based, and anticipatory threats that are not yet officially reported in other literature. These attack vectors are reported in order to assist researchers in preempting vulnerabilities and finding ways to harden protocol specifications and directing systematic security reviews as these ecosystems evolve.

5 Potential Threats derived from Protocol Design and Architecture

While the Threat Model section discussed security threats specifically derived from the literature, this section covers the risks based on the structural and operational characteristics of the protocols themselves. These threats do not appear explicitly in previous literature but are logical deductions in the design decisions, communication patterns, and trust assumptions shaped in MCP, A2A, Agora, and ANP. By separating them from literature-derived threats, we emphasize the novelty of this analysis and the speculative quality of it: they are the possible threats that should be taken into account in future work, although they are not yet officially recognized or even confirmed and validated in the literature. These threats are thus considered as analytical projections and not as established vulnerabilities and are presented in order to inform the future protocol design, assessment, and empirical validation.

This section groups threats by their functional nature and point of impact, similar to the previous section. In functional domain alignment, each group represents a security domain, such as Authentication & Access Control, Supply Chain Integrity, and Operational Reliability. From the threat scope and target granularity point of view, each subcategory captures what aspect of the system is directly attacked. Indeed, authentication-based threats target identity and trust establishment, and supply chain–related threats target ecosystem provenance and update integrity. In this way, operational integrity threats target runtime consistency and availability. The taxonomy is shown in Figure 9.

5.1 Authentication & Access Control

5.1.1 Replay Attack

Replay attacks are carried out by re-executing privileged tasks; in effect, an attacker uses requests or session tokens that have already been successfully used. Nonces, timestamps, or strict session expiration are some of the mechanisms used to ensure that a processed request cannot be replayed. However, in current MCP implementations, there is little discussion of standard mechanisms for request uniqueness. This means that attackers may capture a valid tool call or token and reuse it in the future. This risk is particularly significant in multi-tenant or enterprise systems, where repeating privileged commands can compromise data integrity. Therefore, incorporating nonce encryption, token expiration, and replay detection mechanisms into MCP workflows is important to mitigate this type of vulnerability.

In the case of Agora, messages consist of protocolHash, protocolSources, and body, and the lack of a standard freshness mechanism encourages attackers to monitor or eavesdrop on traffic and reuse a request that was previously accepted in another session. Although HTTPS ensures confidentiality and integrity over the network, freshness is an application layer issue and requires explicit fields and a validation mechanism to reduce repetitions.

A2A has been designed to work with asynchronous and long-running workflows. In this condition, tasks can be kept active over long periods, and agents can communicate periodically regarding their current status. Although this model will improve scalability, it also provides a chance to attack through replay. Unless task messages or tokens have unique nonces, timestamps, or a clear expiry system, an attacker can steal a legitimate request and replay it at a later time to run privileged operations again. An example here is that a replayed workflow approval or artifact submission message may result in a duplicate of a financial operation or an unwarranted execution of a task. Although A2A uses standards like JSON-RPC and HTTP(S), freshness checks at the protocol level are not standardized and provide a window for replay attacks.

5.1.2 Token Scope Escalation

In A2A, the agents typically transmit credentials as tokens that they use to access resources or workflows. To be effective, these tokens can encompass several tasks or grant privileges. On the protocol layer, the scoping of A2A is not strictly enforced; indeed, it is left to the identity and authorization infrastructure underneath to implement fine-grained scoping. It poses a structural risk: an attacker who compromises a token that is supposed to grant access to a limited workflow also has access to expanded privileges, so they can increase the scope of their control after obtaining it. As an example, a token that will be used in document retrieval can also allow document modification and thus allow artifact tampering. In the absence of a protocol-level mechanism to standardize the design of least-privilege tokens, scope escalation is a latent threat amongst implementations.

5.1.3 Privilege Escalation

Privilege escalation is the expansion of permissions that are not meant to be allowed, but an adversary can get them through the exploitation of weak access control or configuration [47]. This is possible in the case of MCP when tools or servers receive coarse-grained permissions, but without a strict implementation of ACLs, malicious tools can execute operations outside of their approved scope. Moreover, the problem of post-update privilege persistence makes MCP more vulnerable since it allows revoked keys to be in use. In A2A, the escalation of privileges stems not from the design of the token scope but from weaknesses in authorization at the workflow level, such as granting control over artifacts or downstream tasks to agents without proper mutual validation. The issue of escalation appears in the context of ANP, where the agents discuss meta-protocols without enforced policies. Rivals can use poor negotiation results to take up positions of greater responsibility. In Agora, fallback to natural-language routines makes protocol semantics open to adversarial manipulation. As a result, it can persuade peers to accept more permissive capabilities.

5.1.4 Identity Forgery and Impersonation

Identity forgery is a type of attack in which attackers register or advertise a fake identity to impersonate a legitimate server, tool, or agent [47]. In MCP, the tool and server discovery relies on free-text names and descriptions without a strong cryptographic binding. Thereby, a malicious actor can mimic a legitimate tool name and mislead clients into invoking the endpoints that are under the control of attackers. In A2A, this threat is related to the federated model of agent cards and JWT-based authentication. So, if an agent card is forged, attackers can impersonate legitimate agents in the entire organizational domain. ANP uses DIDs, but the lack of a centralized revocation and trust anchors provides a risk window for adversaries to mint pseudonymous agents at scale and expand the impersonation across domains. In Agora, agents negotiate PDs in natural language. So, adversarial agents can represent fake capabilities or inject forged PDs to impersonate valid roles. Generally, in all the protocols, identity forgery decreases the trust in discovery and leads to hijacked workflows and unauthorized access.

5.1.5 Sybil Attacks

In the Sybil attack, adversaries create a massive number of fake identities to get disproportionate influence [47]. Sybil attacks destroy trust, distort discovery, and can deny legitimate agents service. In MCP, if attackers register many malicious tools or servers, they can deceive clients and provide difficulty in identifying valid entities. In A2A, the attacker can introduce a large number of pseudo-agents using improperly validated or compromised agent cards; therefore, they can destabilize task assignment or even saturate the coordination mechanisms. In ANP, DIDs can not provide any protection against Sybil generation. It is necessary to have a reputation or staking mechanism; otherwise, adversaries may participate with many pseudonyms and disrupt consensus-driven collaboration.

5.1.6 Cross-Vendor Trust Boundary Exploitation

A special feature of A2A is that it is capable of facilitating the collaboration of agents at the inter-organizational and inter-vendor level. Although this allows interoperability, it increases the boundary of trust. Assuming that one of the participating organizations has a weaker validation of JWTs or poor management of its key distribution, attackers can use that weak point to compromise agents or escalate privileges within other organizations. Since A2A provides a two-way communication scheme where agents promote capabilities through standardized Agent Cards, a compromised trust anchor in one area can spread out and damage the integrity of the whole workflow. A2A, at the protocol level, is based on federated trust but does not specify governance of inter-organizational identity assurance and exposes the boundary between domains to exploitation.

5.2 Supply Chain & Ecosystem Integrity

5.2.1 Supply-Chain Compromise

The external and community-built tools used by MCP give a supply chain attack potential. Like other current ecosystems that are prone to malicious or compromised dependencies, MCP is prone to those due to its decentralized and open-source nature. A malicious actor may breach a common open-source MCP server repository and install a backdoored dependency, or they may target a vulnerable third-party API that is a part of MCP. The impact of these kinds of compromises is that, because MCP servers dynamically load tools and resources at runtime, such compromises may spread across ecosystems with minimal consideration. MCP does not require any central auditing or code-signing requirements, and this enables attacks to exploit the trust of community-provided components. This makes the cost of cascading compromises, which one weak library can impose on thousands of MCP-enabled agents, even more likely to happen. Safe package registry settings, use of reproducible builds, and ensuring dependency attestation will be useful in minimizing supply chain vulnerabilities in MCP environments.

5.2.2 PD Spoofing and Repository Poisoning

Since PDs in Agora are fetched by URIs provided by peers and only integrity is verified through a hash, an adversary with the ability to manipulate where a PD gets fetched may either attempt substitution of the PD (e.g., by providing a different PD at the expected URI) or rollback (point to a weaker previously fetched PD whose hash remains known to the adversary). The absence of authenticity, including signatures, trust anchors, or governance on the provenance of PD, can result in agents that may end up executing routines that embody an attacker’s semantics while appearing syntactically valid. The threat is increased by decentralized storage and lack of a central registry; hash helps to detect bit-level manipulation of the fetched file, but does not help to prevent an attacker from directing you to which PD/hash to trust in the first place.

5.2.3 Protocol Fragmentation Risk

One of the important risks that arises due to the rapid expansion of AI agent protocols is protocol fragmentation. In the case of the proliferation of overlapping protocols, it can result in the formation of redundant ecosystems with uncertain maturity and control. Due to the lack of convergence, an adversary is able to result in a downgrade of less secure or poorly maintained implementations. Riding on such conditions, an attacker will be able to reduce the agent system to a weak or less secure implementation. For example, an attacker can redirect traffic to an old MCP extension that is not properly patched in an enterprise environment running both MCP and A2A. By doing this, the attacker is able to force a downgrade to the system that compromising system integrity and exposing the system to vulnerabilities that have already been fixed. To address this risk, stronger management policies and version alignment are necessary.

5.2.4 Version Rollback

In Agora, the integrity of that particular document is guaranteed by the identification of PDs by hash; however, it does not determine which version is authoritative in the system. The adversaries have the ability to propagate older PD hashes whose schemas allow broader interpretations or weaker constraints. The absence of a policy on the minimum acceptable versions of the PD can cause subdivision of agents between variants of the protocol, effectively spoiling protocol hardening and permitting a scale of downgrade attacks.

5.2.5 Onboarding Exploitation

The first step in the protocol ecosystem is agent onboarding, where tools, agents, or servers are registered, and this needs strong verification, attestation, and governance. In the absence of strong verification and validation mechanisms, this stage becomes a serious and vulnerable weak point in the environment, and adversaries can introduce malicious entities before any security controls apply. This threat is different from impersonation or tool poisoning because it targets the entry point of the ecosystem: as soon as a malicious entity enters the system, subsequent trust assumptions across all protocols are broken.

Generally, the onboarding process in MCP is community-driven, and thousands of tools are presented in open catalogs without cryptographic provenance. This opens an entry for unverified code. In A2A, agent cards are used in the onboarding process, and adversaries embed malicious agents into workflows. In ANP, the IDs are decentralized, which worsens the risk in the onboarding stage. Any entity is able to mint a DID and promote itself as an agent, which is why malicious agents can saturate the ecosystem with low-quality or spoofed agents. In Agora, onboarding exploitation is expressed in PD repositories, and PDs are published without an authenticity guarantee. Malicious actors are able to post polluted or vague PDs, which lead agents to unsafe negotiations. In all the protocols, weak onboarding means weak foundations: when a malicious entity is already within the system, the following trust assumptions are affected.

5.3 Operational Integrity & Reliability

5.3.1 Cross-Protocol Interaction Risks

The MCP is designed to be used alongside other standards and ecosystems, e.g., OAuth when authenticating, REST APIs to invoke tools, or A2A protocols to communicate between agents. Although this interoperability is more flexible, there is a risk when the security assumptions of different protocols are not consistent. As an example, when OAuth tokens are not scoped or expired on a regular basis, both in MCP and external services, attackers can use those differences to gain privileges. Likewise, REST APIs, which are incorporated in MCP workflows, can have less strict rules of validation than MCP itself and provide room to create injection-based exploits or misconfigured exploits. Cross-protocol attacks are also highly dangerous since they take advantage of the interfaces between systems instead of vulnerabilities of one protocol. Because MCP is explicitly in support of modularity and integration, its attack surface is not limited to its own design but to the weakest point between standards interconnected by MCP.

5.3.2 Cross-protocol confusion attacks

This risk arises from poor interoperability between MCP, A2A, Agora, and ANP. Because these protocols have different methods for trust assumptions (tokens in MCP, OAuth2 in A2A, DIDs in ANP, and PDs in Agora), cross-protocol interactions have potential for mismatched security guarantees. Attackers can misuse these differences and relay messages between protocols, bypassing the tighter checks in one ecosystem because of weaker checks in another. For better clarification, consider that a long-lived A2A token can be reused in an ANP setting where no DID-based revocation is implemented, and allows privilege escalation. In the absence of standardization of cross-protocol validation, interoperability is not only a feature but also a potential attack area.

5.3.3 Context Explosion and Resource Exhaustion

The availability and reliability of agentic workflows in A2A and MCP can be compromised through unrestricted output of tools or complex parameter spaces. The output of an adversarial tool in MCP or A2A-mediated chains can be excessively large and overwhelm downstream agents. Since the protocol has a small payload size, the nest level and rate are not applied equally; context explosion is a denial-of-service attack that leads to difficulty in differentiating from normal long-term computing.

5.3.4 Intent Deception

Intent deception is the misrepresentation of the intentions or the ability of an adversary with the aim of achieving unintended influence [47]. In MCP, the tools used by malicious actors may promote deceptive descriptions, e.g., they may pretend to be log analyzers when stealing data. In A2A, the adversarial agents can release agent cards that depict seemingly innocent capabilities and behave maliciously during operation. Intent deception occurs in the context of automatic negotiation in which agents in ANP falsely represent their constraints or service descriptions to attempt to influence task distribution. And eventually, in Agora, intent deception occurs when adversaries present PDs that have concealed adversarial semantics in natural-language statements.

5.3.5 Collusion and Free-Riding

Collusion is a situation where a number of malicious agents join to manipulate results, and free-riding is a scenario where the opponents take advantage of the efforts of others without contributing [47]. In MCP, colluding occurs when various tools support each other in their misleading description in order to overcome discovery rankings. In A2A, malicious agents may create sub-networks of collaborating agents to make deviations in distributed workflows or increase malicious impacts, and free-riding agents receive results without contributing data. Collusion in ANP is one of the most menacing since the meta-protocol provides ad hoc group negotiation, which can be compromised by colluding opponents. Agora is affected by collusion, where there is more than one adversarial agent, and they insert reinforcing PDs to crowd out legal documents. These threats undermine equity and effectiveness in the cooperation of multiple agents.

5.3.6 Semantic Drift Exploitation

Semantic drift is defined as the progressive drift towards differences in the interpretation of terms, embeddings, or ontologies by agents. In a distributed ecosystem, adversaries are able to choose this difference by injecting malicious concepts that are seen in a different way and that corrupt the coordination. In MCP, a malicious tool can produce outputs with ambiguous schema fields or overloaded names (e.g., “/delete”) and deceive some clients into performing malicious actions while others treat them as harmless actions. In A2A, the adversaries may take advantage of the disparities in the definition of capability description in the Agent Cards by federated organizations. A "verifyTransaction" skill can imply compliance checking in one place and financial authorization in another, allowing attackers to use it to escalate privileges. Semantic drift is especially severe in ANP since it negotiates with meta-protocols. Weak schema definitions can be pushed by malicious actors during negotiation that force some agents to accept permissive interpretations that lead to critical data leakage. In the case of Agora, semantic drift may be experienced through the application of natural-language fallback to mediate PDs. The attackers are able to seed ambiguous or malicious fragments of language, which will be interpreted differently by various agents, leading to a cascading failure or security breach.

The summary of all the potential threats in AI agent protocols is presented in Table 5.

6 Evaluation

Risk management in AI agent communication protocols is an important and ongoing process that examines various aspects of security, including identifying, assessing, and mitigating risks. The main goal of this assessment is to reduce security risks to a manageable level, which is possible by identifying the vulnerabilities that are most likely and impactful. This assessment should examine the entire life cycle of AI agent communication protocols to provide sufficient insight into the risks at each stage of the life cycle.

6.1 Assessment Methodology

To effectively assess risks, we need to understand the likelihood of a vulnerability being exploited, as well as the impact of the exploitation on the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of agent interactions. In the context of multi-agent systems and protocol interoperability, "likelihood" refers to the probability of a protocol flaw, weak authentication scheme, or misconfigured token being exploited. "Impact" refers to the potential severity of the resulting damage, for example, risks such as unauthorized access to data, disruption of service, privilege escalation, or agent impersonation.

Following the NIST SP 800-30 [42] risk assessment methodology and ISO/IEC 27005:2022 [27], this study adopts the standard risk formula:

R=L×IR=L\times I (1)

where R is the overall risk, L is the probability of a threatening event, and I is defined as the magnitude of impact. The formula is popular in cybersecurity evaluation systems (e.g., [4]), which has been applied here to evaluate risks in the communication protocols of AI agents.

In this analysis, we employed a qualitative risk assessment approach as the rationale of NIST SP 800-30. All the variables will be rated on a three-level scale, where Low will be rated for rare frequency or minor impact, Medium will be rated for partial and moderate level, and High will be rated for frequent and severe effects. This method is analytical and enables qualitative reasoning across protocols. In order to achieve consistency between various architectures of AI agent communication protocols, qualitative risk levels (high, medium, low) are determined based on protocol-independent reference metrics and not protocol-dependent baselines. In particular, likelihood ratings are conditional on observable factors, like level of exposure, ease of exploitation, and propagation potential, whereas impact ratings are conditional on the measure of loss of control, blast radius across agents, and recovery complexity. These standard metrics are mapped onto the architectural mechanisms of each protocol (e.g., agent-tool invocation, agent-agent negotiation, or policy-based delegation), and therefore, a given qualitative level would have similar security implications across protocols and lifecycle phases. Consequently, a medium rating in one protocol, like A2A, would have the identical severity of a common interpretation of an MCP of the same severity, even where the underlying attack vectors differ.

Since MCP, A2A, Agora, and ANP are still newly proposed protocols with limited public deployments, our evaluation is not based on empirical incident data and reported vulnerabilities. Instead, the ratings of impact and likelihood are based on a systematic, architecturally based analysis derived from protocol specifications, documented design decisions, and observable security control placement. For each vulnerability, we evaluate the intrinsic exploitability, which is done by assessing the requirement of a security control as mandatory, optional, or non-existent, and the scope and propagation capability allowed by the communication and trust model of the protocol. This method is aligned with design-time risk assessment guidelines in NIST SP 800-30 and ISO/IEC 27005, where risk is estimated in situations of uncertainty based on threat model, expert judgment, and scenario analysis, rather than attack frequency in the past.

Based on NIST SP 800-30, risk assessment involves five tasks, including (1) identifying threat sources, (2) identifying vulnerabilities that may result from those threat sources and events, (3) determining the likelihood of their occurrence, (4) determining the magnitude of impact for each vulnerability, and finally (5) assessing risk values for the identified threats. In the following, each task will be described.

6.1.1 Task 1- Identifying threat sources

The goal is to identify all potential threat sources and events that could compromise the security of AI agent protocol ecosystems. A threat source can be an actor, process, or environmental condition with the potential to exploit a vulnerability that could result in loss of confidentiality, integrity, or availability. We have described the sources of threats on an abstract basis, but not on a basis of particular adversary personas (e.g., script kids or state-sponsored actors). This decision is explained by the fact that we intend to analyze the protocol-level exposure and exploitable nature regardless of the sophistication of the attacker. Due to this reason, we make assumptions of a capable adversary who has access to the network in accordance with the planned deployment of the protocol. We then evaluate the protocol design decisions that can be exploited on the assumption. This abstraction is in line with the design-time risk assessment practices described in NIST SP 800-30, where threat capability may be fixed to perform in structural vulnerability analysis.

The origin of threats is classified in four groups that are adopted from NIST SP 800-30 but extended for the AI agent ecosystem:

  1. 1.

    Malicious Human Actors: persons or groups who try for unauthorized access or manipulation.

  2. 2.

    Compromised or Malicious Agents: Legitimate agents or tools that have been hacked and used to perform unauthorized actions.

  3. 3.

    Supply-Chain and Infrastructure Attackers: Adversaries misusing external components that the protocol depends on.

  4. 4.

    Accidental and Operational Sources (Non-Malicious):

    • •

      Configuration Errors: human mistakes during deployment, update, or policy definition.

    • •

      Software Defects: logical errors or implementation bugs that weaken enforcement of protocol guarantees.

    • •

      Operational Failures: unintended disruptions such as version skew, dependency drift, or partial system outages.

6.1.2 Task 2- Identifying vulnerabilities

The goal of this task is to determine the specific technical vulnerabilities that are made by the threat sources determined in the previous task. In this study, vulnerability is a description of a non-existent, weak, or unenforced security control, on the protocol design or deployment level, that facilitates a threat event when it is exploited. These vulnerabilities exist at the design-level or operational-level of protocols and should be explicitly mapped with lifecycle stages to capture and assess risks in each stage of the protocol ecosystem.

The vulnerabilities addressed here were chosen based on them being (i) directly due to protocol specifications or documented design decisions and (ii) controlling risk exposure in at least one stage of the life cycle of the different AI agent communication protocols. To simplify and make the list consistent, the vulnerabilities are categorized based on the stage of the lifecycle they are exposed to:

  • •

    Creation and Configuration Stage:

    • –

      Weak or absent identity verification mechanisms, including shared or static credentials.

    • –

      Lack of integrity protection for registration artifacts (e.g., unsigned or unverifiable registration files).

    • –

      Insufficient namespace isolation, enabling impersonation or naming collisions among agents or tools.

    • –

      Absence of baseline security policy or governance constraints during onboarding.

  • •

    Operation Stage:

    • –

      Lack of mandatory validation or attestation for executable components, enabling the introduction of unauthorized or untrusted executable components.

    • –

      Insufficient control over data exchange, leading to context leakage or unauthorized information flow.

    • –

      Inadequate enforcement of least-privilege principles, allowing privilege escalation via persistent or reused tokens.

    • –

      Missing rate-limiting, quota enforcement, or backpressure mechanisms, enabling resource exhaustion or denial-of-service conditions.

  • •

    Update and Maintenance Stage:

    • –

      Failure to revoke or reissue credentials after updates, resulting in residual privileges.

    • –

      Absence of rollback protection or version pinning, enabling downgrade to vulnerable protocol states.

    • –

      Lack of authentication or integrity verification for maintenance packages or updates.

    • –

      Uncontrolled transitive dependency evolution, leading to configuration drift or inconsistent security guarantees.

6.1.3 Task 3- Determining the likelihood of occurrence

This task aims at determining the probability that the vulnerabilities will be used by the threat sources. The intrinsic exploitability and environmental exposure of each protocol in the lifecycle stages are investigated for likelihood estimation. Intrinsic exploitability reflects the design flaws in the protocol, e.g., not expiring tokens and failure to sandbox. On the other hand, environmental exposure shows operational context, e.g., APIs’ openness and monitoring procedures. Likelihood ratings represent inherent exploitability at the protocol level within the standard conditions of deployment. This method is compatible with the NIST SP 800-30 qualitative risks framework that the likelihood is the combination of both design and deployment context.

The table is a qualitative image of the probability of a weakness being utilized during AI agent communication protocols. When the likelihood is considered to be high, it means that there are conditions that can be readily exploited with few counter-control measures, and when the likelihood is considered to be low, the conditions are mature and they are well-regulated deployments.

Table 6 presents the structured likelihood model that links observable protocol behaviors and architectural properties to high, medium, and low exploitability levels.

6.1.4 Task 4- Determining the magnitude of impact

Impact level is used to assess the severity of security consequences an attacker can cause by effectively exploiting a vulnerability in a communication protocol of the AI agents. We apply a qualitative three-level scale (High, Medium, Low) in line with NIST SP 800 30 [42] and [4], modified based on the nature of operations of multi-agent protocols of MCP, A2A, Agora, and ANP.

Each level indicates the potential extent of damage loss to confidentiality, integrity, or availability (CIA) of the agent ecosystem and the intensity of the harm to the normal operation.

  • •

    High impact is used to show that an exploit triggers consecutive operation failures or a universal service disruption over multiple agents. Such accidents take a lot of recovery.

  • •

    Medium impact is minor yet significant security or performance degradation. The failures are specific to the agents or components and can be addressed by the standard mitigation.

  • •

    Low impact means small-scale disruptions having few security consequences. The effects are temporary and easily reversible and do not compromise overall system performance or trust relationships.

Table 7 presents the detailed indicators of using these impact ratings, which brings the qualitative advice of NIST to the security behavior of current AI-agent communication protocols.

6.1.5 Task 5- Assessing Risk

The last stage of the risk assessment process is to calculate the security risk of each vulnerability that was identified during the previous tasks. This work is in accordance with NIST SP 800-30 [42] and conceptually aligns with ISO/IEC 27005:2022 [27]. The total risk value is calculated based on the interaction between the likelihood (L) of vulnerability occurrence and the impact (I) of that on the system:

R=L×IR=L\times I (2)

So, this formulation covers both dimensions of risk, including the likelihood that an attacker will be able to make use of a protocol vulnerability and the magnitude of the resultant damage to the confidentiality, integrity, or availability (CIA) of the multi-agent ecosystem. We use a qualitative three-level risk matrix to facilitate the comparison of the heterogeneous frameworks like MCP, A2A, Agora, and ANP.

  • •

    High Risk: shows that the exploitation of vulnerability is possible and leads to system integrity loss, widespread operation disruption, or loss of fundamental agent-network capabilities.

  • •

    Medium Risk: represents a vulnerability that makes a local or recoverable disruption in protocol performance.

  • •

    Low Risk: indicates a vulnerability has a little impact on operations, which normally affects only one agent and can be fully mitigated early.

Table 8 is the resulting matrix that gives a comprehensive method for comparing security risk among the various protocols and lifecycle phases and shows how overall risk severity is determined by the interaction between likelihood and impact.

6.2 Lifecycle-Based Evaluation Framework

Despite the fact that individual operational phases, including creation, operation, and update, are only formally specified in MCP, all agent communication protocols tend to act through similar security-relevant states. This study uses a generalized three-phase lifecycle model (Creation/Configuration, Operation, Update/Maintenance) to be able to do inter-protocol comparisons with other models.
