The justification of this is consistent with the NIST SP 800-30 risk assessment process, which identifies threats and vulnerabilities during the system development and maintenance process.

By this framework, the activities of any protocol are mapped to similar functions in the life cycle: Creation/configuration involves identity registration, capability discovery, and initiation (e.g., OAuth setup in A2A, DID registration in ANP, and PD publication in Agora). Operations contain runtime data exchange and invocation of a tool (e.g., MCP host-server execution and JSON-RPC/SSE in A2A). Update/maintenance includes patching, protocol negotiation, and version control (e.g., PD revisions in Agora, token renewal in A2A, and metaprotocol negotiation in ANP).

Using this lifecycle approach, the analysis shows how each of the protocols addresses authentication, integrity, and operational reliability at the same functional levels. In the following, the tables related to risk assessment, including probability, impact, and risk at each stage of the life cycle, are presented for the four protocols: MCP, A2A, Agora, and ANP.

6.2.1 Stage 1- Creation/configuration

The creation and configuration phase is the initial point in time when an AI agent or tool enters into a multi-agent ecosystem. Identity establishment, registration integrity, and initial trust anchors are specified here, and most security vulnerabilities start here, since these safeguards cannot come into effect before this point. During this stage, we analytically compare and contrast the MCP, A2A, Agora, and ANP with regard to how they manage identity validation, component registration, integrity verification, and namespace governance. This part evaluates the probability of an adversary taking advantage of weaknesses at setup, the effect of this attack on the overall system, and the level of risk that it will create in every protocol and represents them in Tables 9, 10 and 11. This systematic comparison points out how variations in the design of protocols, e.g., the open registries of MCP, the OAuth authentication model of A2A, the negotiation-based model of Agora, and the identity layer of ANP, influence the security posture of the overall ecosystem prior to any operational activity.

In the four representative protocols, the most security-important phase of the protocol lifecycle is the creation and configuration phase, since it determines under what underlying trust relations, what identity relationships, and what integrity guarantees that future interactions will rely on. The likelihood, impact, and risk assessments (Tables 9 - 11) are consistent in indicating that this-stage vulnerabilities are highly exploitable with predominantly high consequences, with only some exceptions in ANP.

The results can be explained by three general patterns:

If the enrollment paths are open or weakly authenticated, the risk of information disclosure increases, as seen in the MCP and Agora protocols. Both MCP and Agora allow agents or tools to enroll or declare their identity with minimal integrity checks. As a result, vulnerabilities such as weak authentication and unsigned enrollment have a high probability and impact. An attacker can impersonate trusted components or inject malicious logic before any safeguards are activated.

A2A uses limited OAuth2/JWT authentication and mutual token validation when communicating with agents, which reduces the risk of abuse compared to MCP and Agora. These controls limit an unauthorized user’s access to the privileged token and do not allow system-wide impersonation. However, A2A does not have established pre-deployment integrity features: agent cards are self-read JSON descriptors that are not signed, and there is no global registry to enforce uniqueness. As a result, attacks on agent identity metadata or configuration errors during setup are still possible and may result in local misrouting. These features result in a medium probability and medium impact for all four vulnerabilities, placing A2A in the middle of the risk spectrum related to the creation/configuration phase.

ANP is the protocol alone that offers cryptographically strong guarantees of identity during creation time, impersonation, and namespace collision with low likelihood in compliant deployments. Nonetheless, the distributed and cross-organizational character of ANP implies that in the event where misconfiguration or partial verification does take place (e.g., in a registration policy or dependency update), the resulting effect can be spread across the layers. In general, therefore, ANP is characterized by low-median likelihood and median-high impact, as opposed to a consistent benefit across all vulnerabilities.

In general, the risk analysis shows that there is no protocol with a low risk level for all the vulnerabilities in this stage. Open design choices present the greatest risk to MCP and Agora; moderate and localized risk is present in A2A; and ANP implies a high level of identity assurance, but at the same time has a considerable impact in case of a misconfiguration. These results affirm that the creation/configuration phase is the most impactful period of the lifecycle, as early weaknesses carry on to become systemic and hard to fix in the future.

6.2.2 Stage 2- Operation

The operation phase is where agents are communicating with each other, calling routines, and performing actions. In this stage, the vulnerabilities are no longer the configuration weaknesses but the dynamic interaction threats, i.e., unsafe data exchanges and logic manipulation, reuse of tokens, or denial-of-service. As this stage includes continuous communication and real-time decision-making, the vulnerabilities in runtime isolation, encryption, or authorization directly impact agent ecosystems. In order to measure the protocol’s robustness at any given point in the operational process, protocols are tested at four points of vulnerability, such as malicious or poisoned tools in operation, uncontrolled data exchange, privilege escalation through token persistence, and resource exhaustion/DoS. This discussion demonstrates that the architectural decisions influence runtime security exposure in agent networks.

In the operation stage, agents actively run tasks, share context, negotiate workflow, and, on top of them, rely on long-lived credentials. Because of the nature of this stage, the four protocols have a high level of security exposure. In the previous stage, some roots of trust are established, but in this stage, operational risk is introduced by runtime behaviors, such as dynamic message processing, privilege propagation, or coordination between different agents. The assessment results of this phase, summarized in Tables 12, 13, and 14, show that among the vulnerabilities assessed, MCP and Agora have a high overall risk, and this high risk is due to the lack of runtime code integrity enforcement in MCP and dynamic negotiation based on PD in Agora. Both of these vulnerabilities allow the systemic dissemination of poisoned logic or leaked content. A2A presents a moderate risk across all vectors because OAuth2/JWT reduces exploitability and message-level mediation limits impact, but the downside of this protocol at this stage is that it does not provide any guarantees for semantic validation or strict token lifetime management. ANP exhibits mixed behavior; on the one hand, it has strong DID-based authentication, but on the other hand, the multi-layered dependencies cause the impact to increase dramatically once an attack happens, especially in cases such as privilege escalation and poisoned dependency chains. Overall, the results obtained for the operation phase show that although runtime flexibility is essential for agent collaboration, it is the main security risk factor in all protocols.

6.2.3 Stage 3- Update & Maintenance

The update and maintenance phase is the most crucial stage in the life cycle of AI agent communication protocols. This phase determines how agents evolve, acquire new capabilities, remove outdated components, and sustain long-term trust. Initially, identities and configurations are established, and during the second phase, runtime interactions pose the greatest risk; here, the foundational elements on which agents operate change. Any weaknesses in version verification, dependency integrity, or rollback mechanisms can introduce persistent and systemic vulnerabilities that spread throughout entire multi-agent ecosystems. Therefore, this section aims to evaluate how these protocols handle updates and dependency changes and to assess the likelihood and impact of vulnerabilities. The findings that are shown in Tables 15, 16, and 17 offer a comprehensive understanding of how they prevent poisoned updates, stale credentials, version drift, and inter-layer incompatibilities.

The assessment of the update/maintenance phase reveals that all four protocols are at medium to high risk, and the reason for this trend is the reintroduction of trust dependencies after deployment. Vulnerabilities at this stage arise from operational drift, stale privileges, and weaknesses that have accumulated over time. MCP presents a high risk level; the lack of forced revocation, version pinning, and post-deployment signing are the main reasons for this high risk level, which makes rollback attacks, poisoned updates, and transitive drift possible. Agora also has a high risk due to decentralized PD propagation, as old or fake PDs can spread throughout the network and disrupt the negotiation. A2A and ANP perform relatively better. In the case of A2A, OAuth2/JWT restricts privilege propagation and limits the risk radius, but its stateless backward compatibility still remains as a problem and permits local compromise. ANP is relatively less risky due to its DID/E2E identity anchor and layered signing; however, inter-organizational asynchrony and mismatched transitive dependencies still cause moderate operational disruption. Overall, the update/maintenance phase shows a critical systemic pattern: when agents enter long-term operations, the lack of coordinated revocation and version management increases risk across protocols, making it essential to maintain long-term trust in multi-agent ecosystems.

Taken together, our assessment of the three phases of the protocol lifecycle shows that all of the protocols examined still present security and integrity risks that cannot be ignored. Each protocol exhibits strengths in some areas, but none of them offers complete protection across the entire lifecycle. The first phase suffers from weak identity assurance, incomplete signing, and open enrollment models. The second phase exposes runtime behavior to implicit trust and long-lived credentials. Finally, the last phase reveals some of the most persistent vulnerabilities, including stale privileges, unverified updates, version drift, and dependency asynchrony.

This pattern is not surprising. These protocols are young and rapidly evolving and have only recently moved from experimental tools to real distributed systems. To date, there has been limited research, formal analysis, and adversarial evaluation of these protocols. It is important to note that as agent ecosystems expand and interoperability becomes a practical requirement, trust in these protocols cannot be based on optimistic assumptions or informal security practices, and support for security-sensitive or cross-organizational workflows needs to be given greater attention.

If these protocols are to be deployed in environments with sensitive data or requiring cross-domain coordination, they must address their fundamental vulnerabilities. They must provide stronger identity foundations, mandatory signing and version management, coordinated revocation mechanisms, and so on, so that organizations have the necessary authority to deploy these protocols. In short, all four protocols show promise, but they have structural weaknesses that must be addressed before they can support reliable and secure multi-agent systems at scale. The sooner these gaps are identified and addressed, the sooner these protocols can become reliable foundations for the next generation of agent-based applications.

7 Experimental Case Study

In this section, an empirical security evaluation was conducted to convert one of the hypothesized risks that was introduced in the previous section into a falsifiable claim. To achieve this goal, a minimal yet realistic System Under Test (SUT) was implemented to demonstrate the presence (or absence) of the weakness using repeated trials, controlled conditions, and auditable evidence. The objective is not a speculative critique; it is a measurement-driven proof that a concrete security invariant can be violated under a defensible threat model and realistic deployment assumptions. This evaluation style, including explicit success criteria, controlled experiments, and rate-based reporting, is consistent with rigorous AI/agent security studies [17], [55], [12], and [9]that quantify attack outcomes rather than discussing them only conceptually.

MCP does not standardize a protocol-level mechanism that uniquely and cryptographically binds a tool’s identity to its provider when multiple MCP servers are concurrently available. Therefore, tool identity is effectively resolved using non-unique identifiers (e.g., tool name and description) and client-side heuristics, which introduces an operation-stage tool identity ambiguity titled "Lack of mandatory validation or attestation for executable components." When two servers advertise the same tool name (or indistinguishably similar metadata), the client/orchestrator must resolve the collision via a selection policy. Under plausible resolver behaviors (e.g., ordering, best-match scoring, or tie-breaking), this ambiguity can cause tool/provider misbinding, where an invocation intended for a legitimate provider is executed on an unintended or malicious provider.

In an MCP ecosystem where tool identity is resolved using non-unique namespaces (e.g., name/description/metadata without cryptographic binding to a provider identity), an attacker can register a tool whose name collides with a legitimate tool, causing the orchestrator or client to misbind and invoke the attacker’s tool under realistic discovery and selection behavior.

A scenario is assumed to show this high-impact weakness in MCP. Consider a financial institution that deploys an MCP-integrated AI assistant to support merchant payments. The assistant invokes MCP tools to retrieve merchant details and initiate payment authorization requests via approved payment service providers. The orchestrator gets a user request such as “Authorize a merchant payment via the official bank-approved verified PSP tool.” It then selects a tool advertised by one or more MCP servers and calls it.

Two MCP servers are configured in the client environment; one of them is a legitimate payment service provider exposing the tool payments.authorize_transaction for the bank-approved PSP, and the other one is a malicious MCP server exposing a tool with an identical name that returns valid-looking “approved” responses and emits a distinct evidence marker upon execution. For any invocation targeting a tool from the intended provider, the system must never execute that tool from the attacker provider, even when a colliding tool is present. A single observed violation of this invariant under the stated threat model constitutes evidence that the hypothesized weakness is real in the studied setting.

MCP client resolves tools based on name and description without a cryptographic binding to the provider identity. When the AI agent initiates a payment authorization, the orchestrator misbinds the tool invocation to the malicious server instead of the legitimate one. As a result, the authorization request is sent to an attacker-controlled endpoint, leading to integrity and confidentiality violations in a financial workflow.

A strict threat model is adopted to avoid overclaiming; the attacker has the capability to deploy an MCP server and make it visible through the same discovery surface as legitimate servers, or it can be a previously legitimate one that has added new tools. The attacker does not have the capability to compromise hosts, break cryptography, or perform a network Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack. The attacker’s goal is to cause an invocation intended for a legitimate tool to execute on the attacker’s server.

The system under test (SUT) consists of an orchestrator (MCP client runtime) that performs tool discovery, selection, and invocation, and two MCP servers, including a legitimate one and an attacker’s, with at least one colliding tool. The experimental testbed architecture is presented in Figure 10. The payment task is kept constant across trials, and we vary only the minimal factors needed for causality, including the presence or absence of the attacker server, selection policy (ordering-first, best-match scoring, random tie-break on equal scores), and metadata equivalence.

MCP discovery is typically out-of-band, such as static configuration, local provisioning, or an external registry. This experiment models the practice explicitly via a registry-like directory that contains JSON server specifications (server ID, command, and arguments). The runner loads these specifications, and the orchestrator connects to each server over MCP (JSON-RPC over stdio), issues an initialization, and requests tool advertisements. The resulting tool inventory is cached in a candidate index used during the trial loop. It is essential to note that this experiment is not focused on dynamic discovery bugs; it is about what happens after multiple servers are simultaneously available, which is exactly where binding matters.

MCP v1.25.0 (the latest version at the time of writing) is used in this experiment to ensure that the measured behavior is not a legacy artifact. We also set deterministic seeds for randomized tie-breaking where needed and record (i) the discovery artifacts (tool lists), (ii) selection evidence (scores/ties), and (iii) the invoked server per trial, enabling independent replay and verification of results.

Inspired by the attack success rate (ASR), which is used in recent AI security evaluations such as [55] and [9], we define a new, clear success metric where success is counted over repeated trials as Violation Rate (VR), measured using a binary event. A trial is considered a violation if the orchestrator invokes authorize_payment on the attacker provider while the legitimate server is available.

Violation Rate (VR) is reported as

V​R=#​violationsNVR=\frac{\#\text{violations}}{N} (3)

Where N is the number of trials. In this setting, “attack success” is precisely the misbinding event (wrong server executed), making VR an ASR-style measure specialized to server-tool binding failures.

In the experiments pipeline, the Orchestrator (MCP client) establishes a session with each server and performs initialization and tool list to build a unified tool candidate index across servers, and then executes the constant payment task repeatedly. At each trial, the orchestrator performs several tasks, including selection, invocation, and evidence logging. The selection is to choose among candidate tools with the same name using an agent-like best-match score derived from the user task and tool metadata; if candidates are indistinguishable, it applies a random tie-break. Evidence logging records the chosen provider, score breakdown based on similarity to trust cue, and the violation flag. On the server side, the attacker tool emits an unmistakable evidence marker to confirm that the wrong provider actually executed the call.

Crucially, this evaluation does not depend on a misconfigured endpoint or an accidental registry defect. The only precondition is that multiple MCP servers are concurrently available to the same client context, which is a normal and supported deployment pattern. The vulnerability arises because tool identity across servers is not globally unique nor provider-bound at the protocol interface. Therefore, when two servers advertise the same tool name, the client must resolve ambiguity using heuristics or tie-break rules. The measured VR demonstrates that under plausible resolver behaviors, this ambiguity can be exploited to cause wrong-provider execution.

We evaluate the hypothesis across multiple experiments. The most notable finding across all experiments is that when several MCP servers are available, the client must perform cross-server tool resolution. Since the tool name is not globally unique and there is not any mechanism for binding tools to servers in the face of multiple available tools with the same name, the system enters an ambiguity regime where the orchestrator is able to pick an unwanted provider under realistic resolution policies such as ordering, heuristic best-match, or randomized tie-break.

We demonstrate this ambiguity under three increasingly stronger conditions: (A) explicit multi-server static discovery, (B) registry-style discovery, in which ordering is caused by realistic listing and filenames, and (C) a best-match selection that is agent-like, in which identically similar metadata creates stochastic misbinding. Table 18 summarizes the conditions of different experiments. Collectively, these findings indicate that the bug is not an isolated scoring bug, nor is it a collusion discovery-surface bug; it is a system properties issue of ambiguous tool identity under collisions.

In all experiments, when identical tools are present, but the identity of the provider is not tied to the tool identity, a non-zero VR can be observed. Deterministic first-match resolution generates VR=1.0 when an attacker is visible first, and metadata-based best-match selection generates VR=1.0 with an attacker injecting trust cues into the tool description. Importantly, with the attacker cloning metadata to cause indistinguishable candidates, when we eliminate ordering bias by randomizing tie-breaking, misbinding occurs with VR=0.52 in 100 trials. This shows that the failure is not due to a specific scoring function but rather to a lack of resolution in ambiguity between tools and providers.

A proposed approach to address this issue is to make the tool identity provider-dependent and validated by supported cryptographic certificates/signatures, which we will address in future work.

8 Conclusion

This paper presents the first systematic and focused review of the security of emerging AI agent communication protocols at a time when the pace of industry adoption is much faster than the security maturity of the ecosystem. By bringing together scattered initial results and developing a standard taxonomy of security threats, we show that these protocols share common structural weaknesses in authentication, supply chain integrity, operational reliability, and so on. Specific vulnerabilities for MCP and A2A have already been documented in the literature, ranging from weak authentication and command ambiguity to inadequate token management and insecure login. However, for Agora and ANP, no security analysis has been published to date. However, through architectural reasoning, we identify a diverse set of previously unreported attack vectors, such as semantic drift exploitation and protocol fragmentation, that are based on the nature of their decentralized trust models and natural language-based interoperability.

In order to provide a more practical foundation for secure deployment, we proposed a risk assessment model of a lifecycle based on NIST and assessed threats in the different stages of protocols. Our findings indicate that these protocols are not only subjected to individual attacks but also have some systemic weaknesses due to undeveloped governance, inconsistent identity assumptions, and cross-protocol collaboration. Importantly, we complement the qualitative analysis with a measurement-driven case study on MCP that instantiates an operation stage weakness: when tool identity is not cryptographically bound to provider identity, cross-server tool collisions can yield wrong-provider tool execution under realistic resolver policies. By quantifying this misbinding as a violation rate across controlled trials, we demonstrate how a design-level ambiguity can translate into a concrete, reproducible security failure. These risks are becoming more consequential as AI agents expand to enterprise workflows, multi-vendor environments, and even financial operations. Our analysis tries to inform future researchers by predicting both established and emerging threats in order to develop strong, security-sensitive agentic ecologies.

9 Future Research Directions

Even though this research offers one of the first in-depth analyses of security in the emerging protocols of AI agents, a number of key research gaps are still available. The first gap is related to providing a special security layer for MCP. MCP is the only protocol that has been structured for AI agent-tool communication, but it suffers from the lack of a comprehensive security layer to protect it from many attacks. These are especially challenging for financial or safety-critical processes, where the invocation of the tool may cause a sensitive or irreversible activity. For our future work, we would like to implement a formally defined security extension to MCP that includes cryptographic identity anchoring, ephemeral access credentials, and verifiable permission scoping, making MCP suitable enough to be used in enterprise-grade and regulated settings.

In addition to the security aspect, the other critical research gap is the lack of a privacy-based risk assessment for the emerging AI agent ecosystem. The privacy threats that have not been explored yet include metadata leakage, exposure to multi-tenant contexts, propagation of sensitive data by cross-agents, and negotiation logs, which are privacy-destroying. In our next work, we will provide a detailed privacy-risk assessment framework based on these protocols.

Till now, all the research discussed individual protocol security threats, but in this work, we have demonstrated that MCP, A2A, ANP, and Agora use completely different trust assumptions, authentication strategies, and validation strategies, and this creates a chance of confusion, downgrade, and relay-abuse attacks when they are combined. So, cross-protocol security standards and interoperability hardening are urgently required. The next round of research should involve the development of security profiles to be used in interoperability and uniformity of validation rules across protocols.
